sounds.name: Harmonic Sequence
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 55 guide
sounds.blurb: The 960 plays two related eight-note lines on two oscillator banks, and one control voltage crossfades them through the two filters.
sounds.how: The guide’s showpiece. Row A of the 960 drives the first 921A and its three 921Bs into the 904A low-pass; row B drives the second bank into the 904B high-pass. The 960’s clock, turned into S-triggers by the 961, fires the envelopes. The 992 mixes a slow 921 sine and the third 911 and sends the result to both filters at once: as the low-pass opens the high-pass closes in the same direction of voltage, so the two lines trade places in the mix.

steps.title: Two banks under two rows
steps.why:
Row A to the first 921A, row B to the second; each 921A chained to its three 921Bs. All six SAWTOOTHs into two mixers.
- 960 row A (stage 1–8): 0, 1.25, 2.917, 4.167, 5, 4.167, 2.917, 2.083. Row B: 2.917, 5, 6.25, 7.917, 6.25, 7.917, 5, 4.167. Both ROW RANGEs X1.
- 921A (1) and (2) FREQUENCY −1 (OCTAVE): an octave down.
- 921B (2) +0.06, 921B (3) −0.07, 921B (5) +0.07, 921B (6) −0.06.
- CP3A-M (1) and (2): GAIN 1–3 at 4, MASTER 8.
- 960 FREQUENCY RANGE 5, VERNIER 7 (about 4 steps a second).

steps.title: Two filters, two amplifiers, one clock
steps.why:
Bank 1 through the 904A and the first 902; bank 2 through the 904B and the second 902; both into the third mixer and out. The 960 clock goes through the 961 into S-triggers, and CP35 MULTIPLE A takes them to the 911s.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1, REGENERATION 4. 904B FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1.
- 911 (1) and (2): T1 0, T2 5, E SUS 3, T3 4.5.
- CP3A-M (3) GAIN 1 and 2 at 7, MASTER 8.
- Listen for: two interlocking lines, one dark and one thin.

steps.title: The 992 crossfades the filters
steps.why:
The 921 (slow sine, on AUX at level 6) into 992 CONTROL INPUT 1, and the third 911 through the 992’s attenuated EXT INPUT. The 992 sends the sum to both filters.
- 921 COARSE RNG on SUB, FREQUENCY −3, AUX OUT WAVEFORM sine, AUX OUT LEVEL 6.
- 911 (3): T1 6, T2 7, E SUS 5, T3 6.
- 992 CV SWITCH 1 on, SWITCH 4 on, ATTENUATOR +4.
- Listen for: the two lines slowly swap: as the low line brightens, the high one thins out.

context.m921.frequency: In this sound: how slowly the two lines trade places.
context.m992.attenuator: In this sound: how much the third envelope adds to the filter movement on each step.
context.cp3am_3.gain1: In this sound: the low-pass line’s level against the high-pass line.

tweaks.try: Turn the 960 VERNIER up to 9
tweaks.hear: A faster, more urgent pattern.

tweaks.hear: The slow crossfade stops; only the envelope moves the filters.

sounds.name: Expressive Lead #1
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 55 guide
sounds.blurb: Three sawtooths through the ladder filter, with a vibrato that the 911A holds back for two seconds.
sounds.how: The System 35’s lead with one addition. The trigger for the vibrato envelope goes through the 911A first, which passes it on only if the key is still held after its DELAY TIME. Short notes and quick runs stay plain; a long note blooms into vibrato after two seconds.

steps.title: Three oscillators and the voice
steps.why:
Three linked 921Bs, mixed, through the 904A and the first 902, with the first two 911s on the amplifier and the filter.
- 921B (2) +0.08, 921B (3) −0.1. CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1–3 at 5, MASTER 8.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1, REGENERATION 2.
- 911 (1): T1 3, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 6. 911 (2): T1 3, T2 6.5, E SUS 4, T3 6.

steps.title: Vibrato through the CP3A-O
steps.why:
The 921 through the second 902 into the CP3A-O’s EXT INPUT, and the CP3A-O on to the three DC MODs. The third 911 opens the 902.
- 921 on SUB, FREQUENCY +1, AUX sine at level 10. CP3A-O (1) ROUTING SWITCH 4 on, ATTENUATOR 1.2.
- 911 (3): T1 4, T2 5, E SUS 10, T3 4.

steps.title: The 911A holds the vibrato back
steps.why:
The third trigger goes through the 911A’s upper delay before it reaches the third 911.
- 911A upper DELAY TIME 8 (about 2 seconds).
- Cables: CP35 MULTIPLE A 3 to 911A S-TRIG IN (upper); 911A S-TRIG OUT (upper) to 911 (3) S-TRIG IN.
- Listen for: the short notes stay plain; the long note gets its vibrato after two seconds.

context.m911a.delay_1: In this sound: how long a note must be held before the vibrato starts.
context.cp3ao_1.attenuator: In this sound: the vibrato depth.

tweaks.try: Turn the 911A DELAY TIME down to 6
tweaks.hear: The vibrato arrives after about a third of a second.

sounds.name: Expressive Lead #2
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 55 guide
sounds.blurb: Two pulse waves with moving width, in two layers: the ladder filter, and a thinner band-pass part through the 923.
sounds.how: The guide’s second lead uses both mixers. The first CP3A-M mixes two rectangular waves whose width the slow 921 sweeps through the 921A. Its first output goes to the 904A; its second goes through the 923’s high-pass and then its low-pass, a gentle band-pass. Each layer has its own 902 and 911, and the second CP3A-M mixes them, so you can balance a round lead against a thin, nasal one.

steps.title: Two pulse waves with moving width
steps.why:
Pitch and width from the first 921A to two 921Bs; the 921, through CP35 attenuator 1, sweeps the width.
- 921B (2) FREQUENCY +0.12. 921 COARSE RNG on SUB, FREQUENCY −0.5. CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 at 2.5.
- Cables: the keyboard, frequency and width links; RECTANGULAR (1) and (2) to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1 and 2; 921 SINE through CP35 attenuator 1 to 921A (1) WIDTH IN 1.
- CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1 and 2 at 6, MASTER 8.

steps.title: The main layer: 904A
steps.why:
CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to the 904A, then the first 902 under the first 911, into the second mixer and out.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 2. 911 (1): T1 2, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 5.5.
- CP3A-M (2) GAIN 1 at 7, MASTER 8.
- Listen for: a round, reedy lead.

steps.title: A thin layer: the 923 as a band-pass
steps.why:
CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 2 through the 923 HIGH PASS and then its LOW PASS, then the second 902 under the second 911.
- 923 HIGH PASS 6 (about 630 Hz), LOW PASS 8 (about 2.5 kHz).
- 911 (2): T1 4, T2 6.5, E SUS 6, T3 6. CP3A-M (2) GAIN 2 at 5.
- Listen for: a nasal edge on top of the lead. Balance the two with the second mixer’s GAIN 1 and 2.

sounds.name: Mellow Organ
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 55 guide
sounds.blurb: Three oscillators through the 914 for the organ tone, plus a tuned click and a noise click for the key attack.
sounds.how: The guide builds an organ from three parts, each with its own 902 and 911, mixed in the second CP3A-M. The tone is a triangle, a square and a sine from three 921Bs, shaped by the 914 with only a few low bands up. The fourth 921B, on the second 921A, gives a sine pinged through the 904A with a 500 ms decay: a tuned “tock” at the start of each note. Pink noise through the 904B with a 5 ms decay adds the key click.

steps.title: The organ tone through the 914
steps.why:
CM1A CV 1 goes through CP35 MULTIPLE B to both 921As. The first drives three 921Bs: TRIANGLE (1), RECTANGULAR (2) and SINE (3) into the first mixer, then the 914, the first 902 and the second mixer.
- 914: 125 and 175 at 4, 350 at 5, 500 at 3.5, 1400 at 1, everything else 0.
- 921A (1) WIDTH 5 (50 %).
- 911 (1): T1 0, T2 10, E SUS 10, T3 0: on while the key is held, like an organ.
- CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1–3 at 6, MASTER 10. CP3A-M (2) GAIN 1 at 8, MASTER 8.

steps.title: A tuned click
steps.why:
The second 921A drives the fourth 921B, whose SINE goes through the 904A and the second 902. The second 911 has no sustain, so each note gets a short, tuned “tock”.
- 911 (2): T1 0, T2 6.5 (500 ms), E SUS 0, T3 0.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 3.
- CP3A-M (2) GAIN 2 at 5.

steps.title: A noise click
steps.why:
Pink noise through the 904B and the third 902, with a 5 ms envelope: the key click, kept low in the mix.
- 911 (3): T1 0, T2 1.1 (5 ms), E SUS 0, T3 0.
- 904B FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 2. CP3A-M (2) GAIN 3 at 3.
- Listen for: a little “tick” at the start of each note.

context.cp3am_2.gain3: In this sound: how loud the noise click is.

sounds.name: Percussive Lead
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 55 guide
sounds.blurb: A triangle and a detuned sawtooth with a hard front and a slowly moving filter, made for fast lines.
sounds.how: The same patch as on the System 15. The first 911 gives the amplifier an instant attack and a short fall to a low sustain; the second opens the filter slowly and lets it go over seconds, and the 921 sways it on top.

steps.title: Triangle, sawtooth and a hard front
steps.why:
TRIANGLE (1) and SAWTOOTH (2) mixed into the 904A and the first 902 under the first 911.
- 921B (2) FREQUENCY +0.08. CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1 at 7, GAIN 2 at 5, MASTER 8.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1, REGENERATION 3.
- 911 (1): T1 0, T2 5.4, E SUS 4, T3 5.4.

steps.title: Slow filter movement
steps.why:
The second 911 opens the filter slowly; the 921, through CP35 attenuator 1, sways it.
- 911 (2): T1 7.3, T2 3.8, E SUS 9, T3 8.9. 921 on SUB, FREQUENCY −1. CP35 ATTENUATOR 1 at 1.5.
- Listen for: the line brightens the longer you play.

context.m911_2.t1: In this sound: how slowly the filter opens.

tweaks.try: Turn E SUS on the first 911 down to 0
tweaks.hear: Every note becomes a short pluck.

sounds.name: Space Rock
sounds.ref: From the Behringer System 55 guide
sounds.blurb: A whistling self-oscillating filter swept by two slow oscillators, over wind from pink noise.
sounds.how: The 904A with REGENERATION near the top rings on its own, and the 921 and the first 921B (on LO) move its pitch. Pink noise through the 904B, swept by the second 921B, is the wind. Neither needs the keyboard.

steps.title: The singing filter, swept
steps.why:
The 904A rings at REGENERATION 9.5, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −2; the 921 and the first 921B on LO sweep it.
- 921 on SUB, FREQUENCY −2. 921B (1) RANGE LO; 921A (1) FREQUENCY −6 on OCTAVE.
- CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1 at 9, MASTER 9.
- Cables: 921 SINE and 921B (1) SINE to 904A CONTROL INPUTS 1 and 2; 904A to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; CP3A-M to OUTPUT.

steps.title: Wind
steps.why:
Pink noise through the 904B, swept by the second 921B on LO.
- 921B (2) RANGE LO, FREQUENCY +5. 904B FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 1. CP3A-M (1) GAIN 2 at 6.

context.m904a.regeneration: In this sound: at 9.5 the filter is the sound source.

tweaks.hear: A shrill, piercing whistle.

sounds.name: Berlin Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Tangerine Dream — Phaedra
sounds.blurb: An eight-step bass line from the 960 jumping between the root and its octave, with a resonant filter that drifts slowly open and shut.
sounds.how: The sound of the mid-1970s Berlin school: a sequence that never changes its notes, made to breathe by slow filter movement. The 960’s row A plays the pattern through one 921A and two 921Bs. The clock fires a short envelope on the 902 and another on the filter, and a slow 921, mixed in through the 992, sweeps the 904A across a minute.

steps.title: The pattern on two oscillators
steps.why:
Row A to the first 921A, which drives two 921Bs a hair apart. Their SAWTOOTH and RECTANGULAR go through the mixer to the 904A and the first 902.
- 960 row A: 0, 5, 1.25, 5, 2.917, 5, 4.167, 2.083, RANGE X1. FREQUENCY RANGE 5, VERNIER 8.5.
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −2 (OCTAVE). 921B (2) +0.07.
- CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1 at 6, GAIN 2 at 5, MASTER 8.

steps.title: Short notes from the clock
steps.why:
The 960 clock through the 961 to both 911s: one on the 902, one on the filter through the 992.
- 911 (1): T1 0, T2 4.8, E SUS 0, T3 4. 911 (2): T1 0, T2 4.5, E SUS 0, T3 4.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −2.5, REGENERATION 6.5. 992 CV SWITCH 1 on.
- Cables: the clock through the 961 to MULTIPLE A; MULTIPLE A 1 and 2 to the 911s; 911 (1) to 902 (1); 911 (2) to 992 CONTROL INPUT 1; 992 OUTPUT 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: a bubbling, resonant bass line.

steps.title: A slow sweep
steps.why:
The 921, very slow, into 992 CONTROL INPUT 2: the filter opens and closes over many bars.
- 921 on SUB, FREQUENCY −4, AUX sine at level 7. 992 CV SWITCH 2 on.
- Listen for: the line growing brighter and more resonant, then sinking back.

context.m904a.regeneration: In this sound: the squelch on every step.
context.m911_2.t2: In this sound: how long the filter blip on each step lasts.
context.m921.aux_level: In this sound: how far the slow sweep moves the filter.

tweaks.try: Turn REGENERATION up to 8.5
tweaks.hear: Each step rings like a struck pipe.

tweaks.try: Set stage 8 to SKIP
tweaks.hear: A seven-step loop that drifts against the beat.

sounds.name: Octave Pulse
sounds.ref: In the style of Giorgio Moroder — "I Feel Love"
sounds.blurb: A fast sequence bouncing between each note and its octave, tight and punchy: the pulse that disco and techno grew from.
sounds.how: Each pair of steps is a note and the same note an octave up, so the bass bounces on every sixteenth. The 960 runs fast (range 5, near the top); a very short filter envelope gives each step a click of brightness, and the 902 on EXP keeps the notes tight.

steps.title: A fast octave pattern
steps.why:
Row A, fast, into the first 921A and two 921Bs.
- 960 row A: 0, 5, 0, 5, 1.25, 6.25, 2.083, 7.083, RANGE X1. FREQUENCY RANGE 5, VERNIER 9.5 (about 7 steps a second).
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −2 (OCTAVE). 921B (2) +0.05, RANGE 8’.
- SAWTOOTH (1) and (2) into CP3A-M (1) at GAIN 6, MASTER 8.

steps.title: Tight envelopes
steps.why:
The clock through the 961 to both 911s, very short.
- 902 (1) CONTROL MODE EXP. 911 (1): T1 0, T2 5, E SUS 7, T3 3.5. 911 (2): T1 0, T2 4, E SUS 1, T3 3.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1.5, REGENERATION 3.
- Listen for: a driving, pulsing bass.

context.m960.vernier: In this sound: the tempo. Near 9.5 the pattern runs at about 7 steps a second.
context.m911_2.t2: In this sound: the length of the click of brightness on each step.

tweaks.try: Turn E SUS on the second 911 up to 5
tweaks.hear: A brighter, buzzier pulse.

tweaks.try: Move stage 5 of row A to 2.9
tweaks.hear: The pattern’s third pair now lands a fifth up.

sounds.name: Twenty-Four Steps
sounds.ref: The 960 and 962 together
sounds.blurb: The 962 switches between the 960’s three rows every eight steps, so the sequence runs to twenty-four notes before it repeats.
sounds.how: The 960 has eight stages but three rows. The 962 passes one of its three inputs to its output and moves on to the next each time its SHIFT input fires. Patch the three rows into the 962, the 962 into the 921A, and stage 1’s trigger into the 962’s SHIFT: every time the 960 comes back to stage 1, the 962 moves to the next row, and the three eight-note phrases play one after another.

steps.title: One row first
steps.why:
Row A straight into the first 921A; two 921Bs into the voice, fired by the clock.
- 960 rows A, B and C: three related phrases, all RANGE X1. FREQUENCY RANGE 5, VERNIER 8.5.
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −1. 921B (2) +7 (a fifth up). CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1 at 6, GAIN 2 at 3, MASTER 8.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −1, REGENERATION 3. 911 (1): T1 0, T2 5, E SUS 2, T3 4.5. 911 (2): T1 0, T2 5, E SUS 2, T3 4.5.

steps.title: The 962 joins the rows
steps.why:
Rows B and C into the 962’s other inputs, and stage 1’s trigger into its SHIFT.
- Cables: 960 ROW B OUTPUT 1 to 962 SIG IN 2, ROW C OUTPUT 1 to SIG IN 3, 960 STAGE 1 OUT to 962 SHIFT.
- Listen for: a phrase that climbs through three versions before it repeats.

context.m921b_2.frequency: In this sound: a second oscillator a fifth up, quietly, for a fuller line.

tweaks.try: Press 962 TRIGGER BUTTON 1 at any time
tweaks.hear: The sequence jumps back to row A’s phrase.

sounds.name: Third-Row Rhythm
sounds.ref: The 960’s timing row
sounds.blurb: Row C sets how long each stage lasts, so the sequence plays a rhythm instead of even steps.
sounds.how: With 3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING on, row C’s voltage is added to the clock’s control voltage on each stage: a high knob speeds the clock up for that stage, so the step is short; a low one makes it long. The notes come from row A as usual. The result is a looping rhythm with its own swing, set entirely by knobs.

steps.title: An even sequence
steps.why:
Row A through the first 921A to one 921B, plucked by the clock.
- 960 row A: 0, 2.917, 5, 2.917, 4.167, 1.25, 2.083, 2.917. FREQUENCY RANGE 3, VERNIER 6 (slow).
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −1. CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1 at 7, MASTER 8.
- 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 5.
- 911 (1): T1 0, T2 5, E SUS 0, T3 4.5.

steps.title: Row C sets the rhythm
steps.why:
3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING on, and row C’s knobs set high for short stages, low for long ones.
- Row C: 10, 10, 5, 10, 10, 5, 0, 10. RANGE X2.
- Listen for: a lopsided, looping rhythm with quick pairs and long held steps.

context.m960.timing: In this sound: on, so row C sets the rhythm. Off, and every step is the same length.
context.m960.range_c: In this sound: how much row C changes the speed: X4 makes the short steps much shorter.

tweaks.hear: A more extreme rhythm: flurries and long pauses.

tweaks.try: Turn stage 7 of row C up to 10
tweaks.hear: The long held step becomes a quick one.

sounds.name: Delayed Fifth
sounds.ref: The 911A trigger delay
sounds.blurb: A held note brings in a second oscillator bank a fifth up after a second, so long notes open into a chord.
sounds.how: Two banks: the first plays the note, the second, a fifth up, has its own 902 and 911. That 911 is fired through the 911A, which passes the trigger on only if the key is still held after DELAY TIME. Quick notes stay single; held ones grow into a fifth.

steps.title: The main voice
steps.why:
The keyboard to both 921As through CP35 MULTIPLE B. Bank 1 (921B 1 and 2) through the 904A and the first 902 to the third mixer.
- 921B (2) +0.08. CP3A-M (1) GAIN 1 and 2 at 6, MASTER 8. 904A FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 2.
- 911 (1): T1 2.5, T2 6, E SUS 8, T3 6. CP3A-M (3) GAIN 1 at 7, MASTER 8.

steps.title: A fifth that waits
steps.why:
Bank 2 a fifth up (921A (2) on SEMITONE, FREQUENCY +3.5 = 7 semitones), through the 904B (left open) and the second 902. Its 911 is fired through the 911A.
- 921A (2) SEMITONE, FREQUENCY 3.5. 921B (5) +0.1.
- CP3A-M (2) GAIN 1 and 2 at 5, MASTER 8. 904B FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −6.
- 911A upper DELAY TIME 7.3 (about 1 second). 911 (2): T1 7, T2 7, E SUS 9, T3 6.5.
- CP3A-M (3) GAIN 2 at 6.
- Listen for: the long notes swell into a fifth; the short ones do not.

context.m911a.delay_1: In this sound: how long a note must be held before the fifth comes in.
context.m911_2.t1: In this sound: how slowly the fifth swells in once it starts.

tweaks.try: Turn DELAY TIME down to 4
tweaks.hear: Almost every note gets the fifth, just after its start.

tweaks.try: Set the second 921A’s FREQUENCY to 2
tweaks.hear: A major third instead: sweeter, more like a chord.

sounds.name: Rubycon Cutoff Row
sounds.ref: In the style of Chris Franke — the sequencer player in Tangerine Dream, “Rubycon”, 1975
sounds.blurb: A resonant E-minor bass sequence in which every step has its own brightness, set by a second row of knobs.
sounds.how: The 960 has three rows of knobs, and each row is just a voltage that changes with the stage. Row A plays the notes through the first 921A. Row B goes straight into a second CONTROL INPUT of the 904A, so each stage also opens the filter by its own amount: some notes bark, some stay muffled, and the line gets a phrasing no single envelope could give it.

steps.title: The notes on row A
steps.why:
Row A into the first 921A, which drives two 921Bs tuned up to E and a hair apart. Their SAWTOOTHs go through CP3A-M (1) to the 904A and the first 902.
- 960: ROW A STAGE 1 0, ROW A STAGE 2 5, ROW A STAGE 3 4.2, ROW A STAGE 4 2.9, ROW A STAGE 5 0, ROW A STAGE 6 5, ROW A STAGE 7 6.2, ROW A STAGE 8 2.9.
- 960: ROW A RANGE X1, FREQUENCY RANGE 5, FREQUENCY VERNIER 8.8.
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −2.
- 921B (1) FREQUENCY 4.
- 921B (2) FREQUENCY 4.1.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 5, GAIN 2 5, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE −2, REGENERATION 5.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: 960 ROW A OUTPUT 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app).
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; CM1A TRIG (upper) from 911 (1) S-TRIG IN.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the first 902 is shut until an envelope opens it.

steps.title: The clock plays the envelopes
steps.why:
The 960 clock is a V-trigger; the 961 turns it into the S-trigger the 911s need, and CP35 MULTIPLE A copies it to two of them: one on the 902, one on the filter.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 5 · 140 ms, E SUS 3 · 1.7 V, T3 3.5 · 39 ms.

sounds.name: Moondawn Tempo Surge

sounds.blurb: An Italo octave bass in A that jumps to each new chord you play and starts its riff again from the top.

sounds.blurb: A square-wave C electro bass with octave pops added on top, switchable in and out with one rocker.

sounds.name: Running Double-Time

sounds.blurb: An urgent A-minor ostinato that runs at double speed for one pass, then half speed for the next, like a sprinter catching her breath.
sounds.how: The 962 is used here for its TRIGGER OUTPUTs, not its signal inputs. Stage 1’s OUT shifts it, so it alternates between its two stages every pass of the 960. sounds.name: Cosmic Late Vibrato

sounds.blurb: A singing sawtooth lead whose long notes grow a vibrato half a second in, the way a player leans into a held note.

sounds.name: One-Shot Runs
sounds.ref: In the style of Franco Battiato — “L’era del cinghiale bianco”, Milan, 1979
sounds.blurb: Each chord you play fires a quick rising seven-note run that stops by itself, a glittering flourish on every change.
sounds.how: Stage 8’s MODE on STOP halts the clock whenever the sequence reaches it. The keyboard’s V-trigger (TRIG MODE on BOTH, lower jack) goes to the 960’s OSC ON input, so each key starts the clock again: the sequence runs from stage 1 to 7 and stops. The keyboard’s CV transposes the run. FREQUENCY RANGE 2 runs the clock faster than any steady tempo, twelve steps a second.

sounds.name: Fifteen-Step Ostinato
sounds.ref: In the spirit of Mike Oldfield — “Tubular Bells”, 1973
sounds.blurb: A chiming A-minor ostinato that loops in fifteen steps, eight then seven, so it keeps tumbling over the bar line.
sounds.how: The 962 is used as a gate for a trigger. Stage 1’s OUT, copied by the second mixer’s MULTIPLE A, goes both to the 962’s SHIFT and its SIG IN 1; the 962’s OUTPUT goes to the 960’s STAGE 2 IN. The 962 alternates every pass: when it is on input 1, stage 1’s trigger reaches STAGE 2 IN and the sequence jumps straight past stage 1; when on input 2, nothing passes and stage 1 plays. Eight steps, seven steps, again.

sounds.name: Interface FM Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Heldon (Richard Pinhas) — “Interface”, Paris, 1977
sounds.blurb: A fast, abrasive B-minor sequence with a clanging, metallic edge that stays the same shape on every note.
sounds.how: The 921 at audio rate modulates the first 921B’s pitch through its AC MOD: frequency modulation. sounds.name: Logic Waveform Switch
sounds.ref: In the style of Logic System (Hideki Matsutake) — “Logic”, Tokyo, 1981
sounds.blurb: A bright E sequence that changes its voice every bar: a hollow square on one pass, a tearing synced saw on the next.
sounds.how: The 962 switches audio as easily as control voltages. Two different sounds made from the same oscillators, square waves in one mixer and a hard-synced sawtooth in another, go into its SIG IN 1 and 2; its OUTPUT feeds the 904A. Stage 1’s OUT shifts it, so the sequence alternates timbres bar by bar, the trick of the Moog-programmed Tokyo technopop records.

sounds.name: Long-Note Shimmer
sounds.ref: In the style of Christian Löffler — “Mare”, Greifswald, 2016
sounds.blurb: A warm G-minor pulse in which only the long notes bloom into a glassy octave shimmer; the quick ones pass by plain.
sounds.how: Row C, controlling the timing, makes some stages long and some short. The shimmer, a sine an octave up on the second bank, is fired through the 911A, which only passes a trigger that is still on after its DELAY TIME, about a quarter of a second. sounds.name: Garden Bubble Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Inoyama Land — “Danzindan-Pojidon”, Tokyo, 1983
sounds.blurb: A light, bubbling A-pentatonic sequence that sounds like water dripping into a garden pond, gently swung.
sounds.how: Through the 914, only three neighbouring bands, 700, 1000 and 1400 Hz, are up. As the sequence moves, different harmonics of each note fall into those fixed bands, so every note has a different, vowel-like bloop: the bubbling comes from the filter bank, not from any modulation. Row C adds a lazy swing.

sounds.name: Knob-Drawn Wave Bass
sounds.ref: In the spirit of Bruce Haack — “The Electric Lucifer”, 1970
sounds.blurb: A growling, reedy bass whose waveform is drawn with the 960’s knobs, played from the keyboard two octaves below the keys.
sounds.how: On FREQUENCY RANGE 6 the 960’s clock runs at hundreds of steps a second, so row A no longer plays notes: its four unskipped stages repeat so fast they become one cycle of a waveform, the knob heights its shape. sounds.name: Note-by-Note Timbres
sounds.ref: In the style of Gershon Kingsley — the First Moog Quartet, 1970s
sounds.blurb: A bouncy lead line whose tone changes on every note you play: a sawtooth, then a square, then a triangle, round and round.

sounds.name: Valley of the Wind Strings
sounds.ref: In the style of Joe Hisaishi — “Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind”, Tokyo, 1984
sounds.blurb: A warm, slow-bowed string section in D minor, violins, violas and cellos together, gently shimmering as it swells.
sounds.how: This is what the System 55’s two drivers and six 921Bs are for: a whole section from one key. Each 921A carries the keyboard to three 921Bs, set to 8’, 4’ and 16’ and a few cents apart, like players who are never quite in tune. A second 911 brightens the 904A as the bow digs in, and one slow LFO from the 921, fanned out by the CP3A-O’s three outputs, makes three of the six players drift against the other three.

sounds.name: Sketches Brass Choir
sounds.ref: In the style of Gil Evans — the brass voicings of “Sketches of Spain”, 1960
sounds.blurb: A dark, soft-edged brass section playing a slow Phrygian line in D, with a quiet horn a fifth above and a vibrato that only arrives on held notes.
sounds.how: Five 921Bs make the section: two trumpets a few cents apart, a tuba-like pulse an octave down, a third saw on the second driver and a quiet one a fifth up, the open-fifth colour of a horn voicing. The brass bite is a second 911 sweeping the 904A. The vibrato is the clever part: the 921’s AUX output goes through a 902 used as a modulation amplifier, whose envelope is fired by the 911A late, so only notes held longer than the delay start to waver. The CP3A-O hands that vibrato to both drivers.

sounds.name: Forty-Voice Ah
sounds.ref: In the style of Thomas Tallis — “Spem in alium”, England, c. 1570
sounds.blurb: A soft, breathy choir singing “ah” in G, basses, tenors and sopranos in octaves, rising and falling like a slow hymn.
sounds.how: The 914 fixed filter bank is a set of fourteen fixed resonances, exactly what makes a vowel: a voice is a buzz shaped by fixed peaks in the throat and mouth. Six sawtooths in three octaves, a few cents apart, go through it with the bands around 700 and 1000 Hz up, the two formants of “ah”, and a little 2800 Hz for the ring of trained voices. Pink noise through the 923’s high-pass goes into the 914’s second input, so the breath is shaped by the same vowel.

sounds.name: Epic Minor Eleventh
sounds.ref: In the style of Kamasi Washington — “The Epic”, Los Angeles, 2015
sounds.blurb: A huge, warm minor-eleventh chord on every key, moving in parallel from D to B-flat to C to G, the filter breathing slowly.
sounds.how: With six oscillators, one key can play a whole chord: each 921B is tuned to one note of the voicing (root an octave down, minor third, fifth, seventh, ninth and eleventh), and because they all follow the keyboard through their drivers, the chord moves in parallel wherever you play. The 992 gathers control voltages for the filter: here its EXT INPUT takes a very slow 921 sine through its own attenuator, so the 904A opens and closes over several seconds.

- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 7.
- 921B (3): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 10.

sounds.name: Weightless Filter Walk
sounds.ref: In the style of Marconi Union — “Weightless”, Manchester, 2011
sounds.blurb: A soft, held A-minor pad of fifths whose brightness drifts to a new place every two seconds, on a cycle of five that never lines up with the music.
sounds.how: The 960 doesn’t have to play notes. Here it runs very slowly, on FREQUENCY RANGE 3, and only row B is used: five stages of filter settings, the other three skipped. Row B goes through the 923’s LOW PASS before it reaches the 904A, which rounds off each step so the filter moves without a click. Because the walk has five stages and the chords change every eight beats, the two never line up.

sounds.name: Black Mill Tape Wow
sounds.ref: In the style of Pye Corner Audio — “Black Mill Tapes”, 2010s hauntology
sounds.blurb: A dim, wavering A-minor pad that sounds as if it were found on an old cassette: the pitch sags and rises, the top is dull and a faint hiss sits under it.

sounds.name: Sullen Octave Bloom
sounds.ref: In the style of A Winged Victory for the Sullen — “Atomos”, 2014
sounds.artist: A Winged Victory for the Sullen
sounds.blurb: Long, low string notes in D minor that swell in slowly; if you hold one, a soft octave above blooms out of it a moment later.
sounds.how: Two sections with their own amplifiers. The low strings, bank 1, swell in on the first 911. The octave above, bank 2 through the 923’s gentle LOW PASS, has its own 902 and its own 911, and that 911 is fired by the 911A: the key trigger only reaches it if the note is still held after the DELAY TIME. So the octave only appears on long notes, and only after a breath.

sounds.name: Siren Mirror PWM
sounds.ref: In the style of This Mortal Coil — “Song to the Siren”, 4AD, 1983
sounds.blurb: A glassy, slowly swirling pulse-wave pad in E minor, with a hushed, underwater shimmer.
sounds.how: Four RECTANGULAR waves, two from each driver, get their pulse width from their own 921A. One slow 921 triangle goes through a 995 attenuator into CP3A-M (3): OUTPUT + of that mixer moves the first bank’s width, and OUTPUT −, the same LFO upside down, moves the second’s. As one bank narrows the other widens, so the shimmer is always in motion and never thins out.

sounds.name: Masked Ball Oo
sounds.ref: In the style of Jocelyn Pook — “Masked Ball”, from “Eyes Wide Shut”, 1999
sounds.blurb: A low, hooded choir singing “oo” in E minor, the upper voices trembling over still basses.
sounds.how: “Oo” is the darkest vowel: both its formants are low, around 300 and 900 Hz. In the 914 only the low bands are up, so four oscillators, two at 8’ and two at 16’, come out as a round, covered “oo”. A vibrato from the 921’s AUX output goes to the first driver only, so the upper voices tremble while the basses on the second driver stay still, which is how a real choir sounds: never all moving together.

sounds.name: Hingus Cosmic Sweep
sounds.ref: In the style of Sven Grünberg — “Hingus”, Tallinn, 1981
sounds.blurb: A slow, whistling cosmic pad in C: each note sweeps up through a ringing filter, then hovers, the resonance drifting in long arcs.
sounds.how: The 992 is the 904A’s own control-voltage mixer: three switched inputs and an attenuated EXT INPUT, summed and sent to the filter. Here it carries three things at once: the keyboard, so the ring follows the notes; a slow 911 through a 995 attenuator, for the sweep; and the 921 as a slow sine at its EXT INPUT. With REGENERATION high the 904A whistles, and every one of those voltages moves the whistle.

sounds.name: Gave in Rest Organ
sounds.ref: In the style of Sarah Davachi — “Gave in Rest”, 2018
sounds.blurb: A still, glowing C organ chord of six pipes, swelling in slowly and breathing, with a pure, slightly flat major third.
sounds.how: The keyboard plays no pitch here: neither driver has an input, so their FREQUENCY knobs fix the chord, and the key only opens the 902. The six 921Bs are organ stops: 16’, 8’, a fifth (the quint), 4’, a tierce and 2’. The tierce is tuned to 3.9 semitones, about 14 cents under an equal-tempered third, close to a pure 5:4, so it stops beating and glows. A slow 921 sine at the 902’s second control input is the bellows.

- 921B (3): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 7.
- 921B (4): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 0.

- 921B (6): RANGE 2’, FREQUENCY 0.1.

sounds.name: Cathedral Noise Chord
sounds.ref: In the style of raison d’être — “In Sadness, Silence and Solitude”, Swedish dark ambient, 1997
sounds.blurb: A cold, rushing drone like wind in a cathedral, a dark chord hidden in the hiss, over a low B that never moves.
sounds.how: The 914’s bands are tuned resonators. Feed them noise and each band rings faintly at its own pitch, so turning up 125, 250 and 500 Hz (three Bs, octaves apart) with 175 and 350 Hz (near F) between them pulls a dark, tritone chord out of pink noise. A free-running 921B on 32’ adds the low B, and the 921, very slow, makes the whole thing breathe through the 902.

sounds.name: Strumming Overtone Blur
sounds.ref: In the style of Charlemagne Palestine — “Strumming Music”, New York, 1974
sounds.blurb: A shimmering, blurred C drone made of notes hammered seven times a second, octaves and fifths, ringing over a steady hum.
sounds.how: Strummed fast enough, separate notes stop being notes and become a drone full of overtones. The 960 runs at about seven steps a second, its row alternating C and G with an octave and a high E-flat now and then; a short accent from the 911 on every step keeps the strumming audible. Through the 914, with the middle bands up, the overtones pile up in fixed places and ring. Under it, the second driver with no input holds C and G at a steady level through a second 902.

sounds.name: Osmose Reed Breath
sounds.ref: In the style of Ariel Kalma — “Osmose”, 1978
sounds.blurb: A reedy A drone with a fourth below it and the hiss of a forest, the whole sound breathing in and out every five seconds without ever stopping for air.
sounds.how: Circular breathing never stops, but the tone still moves with the breath. One very slow 921 sine, from its AUX output, goes into CP35 MULTIPLE B, and its three copies go three ways at three depths: through a 995 attenuator and CP3A-O (1) to the pitch (a tiny sway), through the 992 to the 904A (a change of colour), and through another 995 attenuator to the 902 (a swell). Everything rises and falls together, as if it were breathing.

sounds.name: Viking Canon Rows

sounds.blurb: A gentle three-voice round in C: the same eight-note tune in three octaves, each voice starting it at a different point, so it chases itself.

sounds.name: Two-Clock Phase Drift

sounds.how: Phasing needs two clocks that almost agree. The 960’s clock plays its row on the first voice. sounds.name: Get at the Wave Loops
sounds.ref: In the style of Takashi Kokubo — “Get at the Wave”, Tokyo, 1987
sounds.blurb: A calm, glinting F-major pattern of seven notes, each played in a different voice: a low sine, a soft triangle, a high bell, never the same note in the same voice for a long while.
sounds.how: Two loops of different lengths. The 960 runs seven stages (stage 8 skipped) of pitch. sounds.name: Sunreturn Trigger Echo
sounds.ref: In the style of Michael Garrison — “In the Regions of Sunreturn”, Oregon, 1979
sounds.blurb: A spacey E-minor sequence in which every note is struck three times, each strike softer, like a note bouncing away down a long echo.
sounds.how: There is no delay unit on a System 55, but the 911A can delay triggers. Each clock trigger fires the first 911 at once and the 911A; with COUPLING on SERIES, the upper delay fires the second 911 a sixth of a second later and the lower one fires the third after the same again. Three 902s take the same filtered sound from CP35 MULTIPLE B, each opened by one 911, and CP3A-M (3) mixes them at falling levels: an echo made of envelopes.

sounds.name: Ritournelle Ostinato
sounds.ref: In the style of Sébastien Tellier — “La Ritournelle”, Paris, 2004
sounds.blurb: A gentle, rolling keyboard ostinato over warm string chords that change from F to C halfway round.
sounds.how: One sequence, two speeds. Row A changes on every stage, the ostinato. Row B holds the same value for four stages, then another for four, so on the second bank it moves only twice per pass: a chord change. And the second bank is a chord on its own: three 921Bs tuned to a root, a third and a fifth, so row B moves a whole major triad, held open by its 902’s FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE.

steps.title: The ostinato

sounds.name: Tremolo-Picked Glow
sounds.ref: In the style of Explosions in the Sky — “Your Hand in Mine”, Texas, 2003

sounds.name: Chapi Chapo Music Box
sounds.ref: In the style of François de Roubaix — “Chapi Chapo”, French children’s television, 1974
sounds.blurb: A tinkling C-major music-box waltz, six notes to the turn, with a lilt on the first beat of each bar and a slight warble of an old toy.

sounds.name: Spectrum Suite Tines
sounds.ref: In the style of Steven Halpern — “Spectrum Suite”, 1975
sounds.blurb: A soft, glowing electric piano in E minor: each note starts with a gentle bell-like bark that melts into a pure, round tone.
sounds.how: An electric piano’s tine is bright for a moment and then almost a sine. Here a second 921B, at the same pitch, frequency-modulates the first through its AC MOD, but it gets there through the second 902, opened by its own fast 911. So the modulation is strong at the start of the note and gone a moment later: a 902 used as a modulation amplifier, not for the sound you hear.

sounds.name: Organic Music Harmonium
sounds.ref: In the style of Don Cherry — “Organic Music Society”, Sweden, 1972
sounds.blurb: A reedy harmonium playing a modal D melody over its own held drone of D and A, the whole instrument pumping softly with the bellows.
sounds.how: A harmonium has drone stops that sound while you play. So the melody is one bank, played from the keyboard through the first 902; the drone is the other bank with nothing at its driver’s input, through the second 902 held open by its FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE. The bellows is one slow 921B on LO, through a 995 attenuator into CP35 MULTIPLE A, whose copies reach both 902s, so melody and drone breathe together.

sounds.name: Fade Into Organ
sounds.ref: In the style of Mazzy Star — “Fade Into You”, 1993
sounds.blurb: A soft, sleepy organ in A, its notes held long and pulsing slowly with a deep tremolo.
sounds.how: A drawbar organ adds sines at fixed footages, and the System 55’s 921Bs are named in footages for exactly that reason. Here 16’, 8’, 4’ and the 2⅔’ quint (4’ tuned up a fifth) are mixed like drawbars. The 921’s AUX OUT, a sine whose level is set right on the 921, goes straight into the 902’s second control input as a slow, deep tremolo: no attenuator needed.

sounds.name: Sunken Cathedral Chord
sounds.ref: In the style of Claude Debussy — “La cathédrale engloutie”, 1910
sounds.blurb: Great, slowly dying bell-chords of open fifths and octaves in G, moving in parallel, with the slightly sour ring of real bells.
sounds.how: Six 921Bs make an open chord on every key: octaves and fifths from 16’ to 2’, like the parallel chords that rise out of the sea in Debussy’s prelude. A struck envelope lets them ring away. What makes it a bell is one more partial: a real bell has a minor third in it, a little sharp. The second bank’s link chain doesn’t stop at the third 921B: its LINK FREQ (to next) goes on into the 921, set to 4’ and tuned up 3.2 semitones, so it follows the keyboard too, ringing that bell partial on its own shorter envelope.

sounds.name: Sonambient Rods
sounds.ref: In the style of Harry Bertoia — “Sonambient”, Pennsylvania, 1970s
sounds.blurb: Slow strikes on a cluster of metal rods: a bright clang that blooms into a long, shimmering, beating hum.
sounds.how: A metal rod’s overtones are not a harmonic series, which is why it doesn’t sound like a note. Here six 921Bs are tuned to six unrelated partials, a few cents and odd fractions of semitones apart, struck by one 911 with a long decay. The two lowest partials, 0.3 of a semitone apart, beat slowly, and a slow 921 wobble on one high partial makes the hum shimmer, as Bertoia’s rods did when they swayed.

sounds.name: Taj Mahal Flute Echoes
sounds.ref: In the style of Paul Horn — “Inside the Taj Mahal”, Agra, 1968
sounds.blurb: A breathy flute in G playing slow phrases, each held note answered by two softer, darker swells of itself, as if a great dome were singing it back.
sounds.how: The sound is split three ways by CP3A-M (2)’s MULTIPLE A: straight to the first 902, through the 923’s LOW PASS to the second, and through the 904A, darker still, to the third. The key trigger fires the first 911 at once and goes into the 911A, COUPLING on SERIES: a third of a second later it fires the second 911, and the same again later the third. Each answer is softer and duller than the last, like sound coming back from further away.

sounds.name: Symphonia Chant
sounds.ref: In the style of Hildegard von Bingen — “Symphonia”, Rhineland, 12th century
sounds.blurb: A single voice chanting a slow D-Dorian line on “oh”, over a second voice holding the low D, as in a medieval drone.
sounds.how: Both voices go through the 914, so both sing the same vowel. The melody is the first bank, played from the keyboard into one input; the drone (the ison) is the second bank with nothing at its driver’s input, through a 995 attenuator into the 914’s second input, the two inputs adding. The 914’s bands around 500 and 700 Hz give “oh”. The first 902 has a little FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE, so the drone never quite stops between phrases, and a light vibrato goes to the melody only.

sounds.name: Itsuki Lullaby Ocarina
sounds.ref: In the style of a Japanese komoriuta — the old lullabies, such as “Itsuki no Komoriuta” from Kumamoto
sounds.blurb: A soft, hollow ocarina singing a slow, sad lullaby in the old Japanese scale, each note starting with a tiny puff of breath.
sounds.how: An ocarina is almost a pure sine, so the character is all in the start of the note: a little chiff of breath as the air hits the edge. That is a second voice: pink noise through the 923’s HIGH PASS into the second 902, opened by the second 911 for an instant only. The two 902s mix in CP3A-M (3).

steps.title: A hollow tone
steps.why:
CM1A CV 1 to the first 921A: a SINE and a whisper of TRIANGLE through CP3A-M (1) and the first 902 into CP3A-M (3).
- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 0.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 6, GAIN 2 1.5, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 911 (1): T1 4 · 60 ms, T2 7 · 780 ms, E SUS 9 · 5.0 V, T3 6 · 330 ms.
- CP3A-M (3): GAIN 1 8, GAIN 2 5, MASTER GAIN 9.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) TRIANGLE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to CP3A-M (3) INPUT 1; CP3A-M (3) OUTPUT + 1 to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + from OUTPUT L (app).
- Listen for: a soft, pure, hollow tone.

steps.title: A puff of breath

sounds.name: Sketch for Summer Swells
sounds.ref: In the style of The Durutti Column — “Sketch for Summer”, Manchester, 1980
sounds.blurb: Delicate, swelling E-major notes with no attack, each one blooming in already mellow, like a guitar played with the volume knob.
sounds.how: Two envelopes working against each other. The first 911, on the 902, rises slowly: the note fades in with no pluck. The second, fired at the same time on the 904A, is a fast pluck that has almost died away by the time the note is heard. So the sound arrives already mellowing, the backwards, glowing quality of volume-swell guitar.

steps.title: A guitar-ish tone
steps.why:
CM1A CV 1 to the first 921A: two SAWTOOTHs and a square RECTANGULAR, through CP3A-M (1), the 904A and the first 902, which swells in slowly.
- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 0.1.
- 921B (3): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY −0.1.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 3, GAIN 2 3, GAIN 3 2, MASTER GAIN 7.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0.5, REGENERATION 2.
- 911 (1): T1 6 · 330 ms, T2 7 · 780 ms, E SUS 8 · 4.4 V, T3 7 · 780 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (2) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (3) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) RECTANGULAR to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; 921B (3) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 3; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.

sounds.name: Pan’s People Chimes
sounds.ref: In the style of The Focus Group — “We Are All Pan’s People”, Ghost Box, 2007
sounds.blurb: A small, eerie five-note chime pattern with a metallic, out-of-tune ring, like an old schools-programme ident half remembered.
sounds.how: A 902’s control input can take audio. Here the second 902 gets the melody oscillator at its SIG IN and a free-running sine at its CONTROL INPUT 1, so the gain follows the sine up and down hundreds of times a second: amplitude modulation. Because the gain stops at 0 V, only the top half of the sine gets through, so the melody keeps sounding and gains clangorous sidebands that don’t belong to its key. The 923’s LOW PASS then dulls it like an old record.

steps.title: A five-note sequence
steps.why:

- 960: ROW A STAGE 1 0, ROW A STAGE 2 2.1, ROW A STAGE 3 2.9, ROW A STAGE 4 5, ROW A STAGE 5 4.2.
- 960: STAGE 6 MODE SKIP, STAGE 7 MODE SKIP, STAGE 8 MODE SKIP.
- 960: ROW A RANGE X1, FREQUENCY RANGE 5, FREQUENCY VERNIER 5.2.
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY 0.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 6.5 · 510 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: 960 ROW A OUTPUT 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SINE to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); 960 OSCILLATOR OUTPUT to 961 V-TRIG IN A (left) 1; 961 S-TRIG OUT (left) to CP35 MULTIPLE A (in); CP35 MULTIPLE A 1 to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; CM1A TRIG (upper) from 911 (1) S-TRIG IN.
- Listen for: a pure, simple chime pattern.

steps.title: Ring it through a 902
steps.why:
Unplug the SINE from the first 902. It goes to the second 902’s SIG IN +; the fourth 921B, free-running at 4’, sends its SINE to that 902’s CONTROL INPUT 1; the second 902’s OUTPUT into the first.
- 921B (4): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 3.3.
- Cables: 921B (1) SINE to 902 (2) SIG IN +; 921B (4) SINE to 902 (2) CONTROL INPUT 1; 902 (2) SIG OUT + to 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Unplug: 921B (1) SINE from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: the chimes turned clangy and eerie, a fixed metallic ring under every note.

steps.title: An old record

- Cables: 902 (1) SIG OUT + to 923 LOW PASS IN; 923 LOW PASS OUT to OUTPUT L (app).

sounds.name: Hybrid Infinite Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Michael Brook — the “Infinite Guitar” on “Hybrid”, 1985
sounds.blurb: A singing, endlessly sustaining E lead whose held notes slowly bloom, until a pure harmonic a twelfth above rises out of them like feedback.
sounds.how: An infinitely sustaining guitar does two things on a long note: its tone blooms, then it tips over into a higher harmonic. The bloom is a slow 911 opening the 904A, its REGENERATION high so the peak sings. The harmonic is a SINE at 4’ a fifth up (the third harmonic) on its own 902, fired through the 911A, so it only arrives on notes held over a second. A 921 vibrato on the driver moves both.

steps.why:

- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 0.1.
- 921B (3): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 7.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 4, GAIN 2 4, MASTER GAIN 7.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 0, REGENERATION 8.
- 911 (1): T1 4 · 60 ms, T2 8 · 1.8 s, E SUS 9 · 5.0 V, T3 7.5 · 1.2 s.
- CP3A-M (3): GAIN 1 8, GAIN 2 4, MASTER GAIN 9.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (2) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (3) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to CP3A-M (3) INPUT 1; CP3A-M (3) OUTPUT + 1 to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to CP35 MULTIPLE B (in); CP35 MULTIPLE B 1 to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.

steps.title: The bloom
steps.why:

sounds.name: Odisea Glass Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Suso Saiz — “Odisea”, Madrid, 1990
sounds.blurb: A glassy, slowly turning C pad: a pure tone with a ghostly cluster of overtones gliding through it, softened as if seen through frosted glass.
sounds.how: Hard sync makes a second oscillator restart with every cycle of the first, so whatever its own pitch, it stays locked to the note, and changing that pitch sweeps its overtones instead of detuning it. The 921, very slow, moves the synced 921B’s pitch through its DC MOD, so a band of overtones drifts slowly up and down. Mixed under a sine and softened by the 923’s LOW PASS, it sounds like light moving in glass.

steps.title: A sine and a synced saw
steps.why:
CM1A CV 1 to the first 921A and three 921Bs: a SINE, a SAWTOOTH a fifth up synced hard to the first, and a quiet SINE two octaves up. The first one’s SAWTOOTH into the second’s SYNC IN. Through CP3A-M (1), the 923’s LOW PASS and the first 902.
- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 7, SYNC STRONG.
- 921B (3): RANGE 2’, FREQUENCY 0.1.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 5, GAIN 2 2, GAIN 3 1.5, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 923 LOW PASS 7.5 · 1.8 kHz.
- 911 (1): T1 7 · 780 ms, T2 8 · 1.8 s, E SUS 9 · 5.0 V, T3 8.5 · 2.8 s.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (2) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (3) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SAWTOOTH to 921B (2) SYNC IN; 921B (1) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) SAWTOOTH to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; 921B (3) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 3; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 923 LOW PASS IN; 923 LOW PASS OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a soft tone with a bright, buzzy edge, locked to the note.

steps.title: Light moving through it

The 921 on SUB, one cycle every three seconds; its AUX OUT 1 into the second 921B’s DC MOD.

sounds.name: Selbstportrait Organ Loop
sounds.ref: In the style of Hans-Joachim Roedelius — “Selbstportrait”, Forst, 1979
sounds.blurb: A homely, gentle organ loop in G of seven notes that jumps up an octave and back every few seconds, never at the same point in the tune.
sounds.how: The CP3A-O adds control voltages before they reach a driver. Row A, seven stages, goes into one of its control inputs; the 921’s RECTANGULAR, very slow, goes into its EXT INPUT, the ATTENUATOR at 1: a tenth of ±5 V, so a step of exactly one volt, an octave. The loop is seven steps long and the square has its own slow clock, so the octave jumps land somewhere new each time.

steps.title: A seven-note organ loop
steps.why:
Row A, seven stages, into CP3A-O (1)’s CONTROL INPUT 1; its OUTPUT 1 to the first 921A: a SINE and a RECTANGULAR an octave up, through CP3A-M (1) and the first 902. The clock fires the first 911.
- 960: ROW A STAGE 1 0, ROW A STAGE 2 1.7, ROW A STAGE 3 2.9, ROW A STAGE 4 3.8, ROW A STAGE 5 2.9, ROW A STAGE 6 1.7, ROW A STAGE 7 0.8.
- 960 STAGE 8 MODE SKIP.
- 960: ROW A RANGE X1, FREQUENCY RANGE 5, FREQUENCY VERNIER 6.
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −1.
- 921B (1): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 7.
- 921B (2): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 7.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 5, GAIN 2 2, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 911 (1): T1 1 · 5 ms, T2 5 · 140 ms, E SUS 6 · 3.3 V, T3 4 · 60 ms.
- Cables: 960 ROW A OUTPUT 1 to CP3A-O (1) CONTROL INPUT 1; CP3A-O (1) OUTPUT 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) RECTANGULAR to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); 960 OSCILLATOR OUTPUT to 961 V-TRIG IN A (left) 1; 961 S-TRIG OUT (left) to CP35 MULTIPLE A (in); CP35 MULTIPLE A 1 to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; CM1A TRIG (upper) from 911 (1) S-TRIG IN.
- Listen for: a simple, sweet organ loop.

steps.title: An octave jump on its own clock
steps.why:
The 921 on SUB, one cycle every three seconds; its RECTANGULAR into CP3A-O (1)’s EXT INPUT, switch 4 on, ATTENUATOR 1.

- Cables: 921 RECTANGULAR to CP3A-O (1) EXT INPUT.
- Listen for: the loop leaping up an octave and back down, out of step with the tune.

sounds.name: Lux Accent Row
sounds.ref: In the style of Clint Mansell — “Lux Aeterna”, from “Requiem for a Dream”, 2000
sounds.blurb: A tense, driving string ostinato in C minor, the same few notes going round, with some leaning harder than others.
sounds.how: Row A plays the notes on three sawtooths, two on the first driver and a cello an octave down on the second, which takes ROW A OUTPUT 2. Row B is not a pitch at all: it goes into the 902’s second control input, adding to the envelope, so its knobs set how hard each stage is played. The dynamics of the phrase are drawn on the 960, stage by stage.

steps.title: A string ostinato
steps.why:
Row A into the first 921A (two SAWTOOTHs) and, from ROW A OUTPUT 2, into the second 921A (a SAWTOOTH an octave down). Through CP3A-M (1), the 904A and the first 902. The clock fires the first 911.
- 960: ROW A STAGE 1 2.9, ROW A STAGE 2 3.3, ROW A STAGE 3 5, ROW A STAGE 4 3.3, ROW A STAGE 5 2.9, ROW A STAGE 6 3.3, ROW A STAGE 7 5, ROW A STAGE 8 1.2.
- 960: ROW A RANGE X1, FREQUENCY RANGE 5, FREQUENCY VERNIER 7.2.
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −1.
- 921A (2) FREQUENCY −2.
- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 0.1.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 3, GAIN 2 3, GAIN 3 3, MASTER GAIN 7.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 1.5, REGENERATION 1.

sounds.name: Human Machine Kit
sounds.ref: In the style of Jaki Liebezeit — Can, “Halleluhwah”, Cologne, 1971
sounds.blurb: A tight, hypnotic drum kit: a deep kick on the syncopated eighths, a crisp snare on the backbeats and a hi-hat ticking on every step.
sounds.how: The 960 becomes a drum machine. Each stage’s OUT is +5 V only while that stage plays, so patching a stage’s OUT fires a drum on that step: three stage OUTs into the 961’s left side make the kick’s rhythm, two into its right side the snare’s. With both halves of the 961 used, the hi-hat gets its trigger from a mixer: the clock and −6 V summed and turned upside down at CP3A-M (3)’s OUTPUT − is a working S-trigger. No 921A anywhere: each drum is a 921B with nothing at its LINK FREQ, sitting at a fixed pitch.

steps.title: A kick on stages 1, 4 and 6

Stages 1, 4 and 6 OUT into three of the 961’s left V-TRIG IN A jacks; its S-TRIG OUT fires the first 911. The kick is the first 921B at 32’, its SINE through the first 902 into CP3A-M (1). The 911 is split by CP35 MULTIPLE B: one copy opens the 902, the other goes through 995 (1) attenuator 1 into the 921B’s DC MOD, so every hit starts high and drops.

sounds.name: Bossa Rim Clave
sounds.ref: In the style of Milton Banana — the drums on “Getz/Gilberto”, 1964
sounds.blurb: A soft bossa nova groove: woody rim clicks playing the lopsided bossa clave over a gentle low bass drum.
sounds.how: The bossa nova clave is five clicks spread unevenly over two bars: three, three, four, three and three sixteenths apart. Five stages play it, the rest on SKIP, and 3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING sets each stage’s length: row C adds to the clock’s speed, so the three-sixteenth stages get 2.1 (about a third faster) and the four-sixteenth stage 0. The clock fires a click on every stage; stages 1 and 3 OUT also fire the bass drum.

sounds.name: One Drop Rim and Kick
sounds.ref: In the style of Carlton Barrett — The Wailers, “Natty Dread”, Kingston, 1974
sounds.blurb: A laid-back reggae one drop: kick and rim click land together only on the third beat, under lazily swung, accented hi-hats.
sounds.how: In the one drop the first beat is left empty and the kick and the cross-stick land together on beat three. That is a single stage OUT: stage 5 fires the 961, whose S-trigger CP35 MULTIPLE A splits to two 911s, one for the kick and one for the rim. The hats play on every step, and row C swings them: odd stages long, even stages short. Row B adds a little to the hats’ 902 on the off-beats, accenting them.

sounds.name: Odaiko Double Stroke
sounds.ref: In the style of Kodo — Sado Island taiko ensemble, “Monochrome”, 1981
sounds.blurb: A huge, booming taiko pattern: the big odaiko answers itself with a second stick a moment after each strike, over a tight, high shime drum ticking every step.
sounds.how: The odaiko fires on stages 1, 3 and 5 of a six-stage loop. Its S-trigger is split by CP35 MULTIPLE A: one copy fires the first 911 at once; the other goes into the 911A, which passes it on 0.12 s later to the second 911. Both 911s open the same 902, the second through an attenuator, so each strike is a heavy DON followed by a lighter ko: the second stick. The shime ticks on every step from the clock through the 961’s right side.

sounds.name: Ringing Filter Congas
sounds.ref: In the style of Mongo Santamaría — “Afro Blue”, 1959
sounds.blurb: A rolling conga tumbao: soft tones, a cracking slap and two open, bending low tones at the end of every bar.
sounds.how: There is no oscillator in this drum. The 904A with REGENERATION at 10 rings on its own as a sine at its cutoff, and the cutoff follows its control inputs at an octave per volt, so row A tunes the drum on every stage. The 902 cuts the ringing into strokes, and its 911 also goes into the 904A through an attenuator, so each stroke starts a little sharp and settles, as a hand on a conga head does. Row B adds to the 902 for the slaps and open tones.

sounds.name: Gated Tom Fill
sounds.ref: In the style of Phil Collins — the drum fill in “In the Air Tonight”, 1981
sounds.blurb: A thunderous descending tom fill, four drums two strokes each, every stroke swallowed by a burst of noise that cuts off dead.
sounds.how: Row A tunes four toms, high to low, two strokes each, into the first 921A. The famous sound is the gated reverb: a big tail chopped off short. Here the tail is noise through the 904A, which follows row A too, on a second 911 with a long decay and T3 at 0. The 960’s clock is high for 90 % of each step, so the 961’s S-trigger ends just before the next stroke and T3 at 0 cuts the tail off dead: the clock’s own gate is the gate.

sounds.blurb: An electro beat: a long, booming kick and a sharp, splashy hand clap on the backbeats.
sounds.how: A drum machine’s clap is not one burst of noise but three or four a few milliseconds apart, the hands of a crowd not quite together, and then a short tail. Here the clap’s S-trigger fires the second 911 at once and goes into the 911A on PARALLEL, whose two delays fire the third 911 10 ms later and the fourth 24 ms later. All three 911s open the same 902 on band-passed noise: three bursts, the last with a longer tail.

sounds.name: Two-Square Cowbell

Here they are two 921Bs with nothing at their LINK FREQ, so the keyboard does not move them: about 540 Hz and 800 Hz, the pair a famous drum machine uses. Their RECTANGULARs go through the 904B to lose the bottom and the 904A to round the top. Two 911s shape it: the first a quick, loud clank, the second, through an attenuator, the quieter ring after it.

sounds.name: Kebyar Ombak Bells
sounds.ref: In the style of Balinese gong kebyar — the gamelan of Bali, as heard on “Music of Bali”
sounds.blurb: A fast, glittering pelog figure on bronze bars that shimmer and beat, with a deep gong blooming under it every other cycle.
sounds.how: Balinese gamelan instruments come in pairs tuned a few hertz apart, so every note shimmers with a fast beating called ombak. Here the bar is two 921Bs a fifth of a semitone apart, plus an inharmonic partial, played by row A. The gong uses the 962 as a divider: stage 1 OUT shifts it every cycle, so its TRIGGER OUTPUT 2 is high every other cycle, and that fires the gong.

sounds.name: Steel Pan Bloom
sounds.ref: In the style of Ellie Mannette — the tuned steel pan of Trinidad, 1950s
sounds.blurb: A bright, singing steel pan playing a sunny calypso melody in F, each note ringing with a sweet octave that blooms a moment after the stick lands.
sounds.how: A tuned pan note has its fundamental, a strong octave and a twelfth. What gives the pan its sung, slightly wah-like attack is that the octave swells up a moment after the strike. So the octave is on its own 902, opened by the second 911, and that 911 is fired by the 911A 30 ms after the key: the fundamental speaks first and the octave blooms after.

sounds.name: Swing Xylophone
sounds.ref: In the style of Red Norvo — “Dance of the Octopus”, 1933
sounds.blurb: A hard, dry, woody xylophone running nimble swing lines in G, each note a crisp click and a short ring.
sounds.how: A xylophone bar sounds an octave above the written note, with a strong partial a twelfth above that, and it dies quickly. Here each part has its own 902 and 911: the 4’ fundamental rings longest, the 2’ twelfth shorter, and a burst of WHITE NOISE through the 923’s HIGH PASS shortest of all, the mallet hitting rosewood. One key trigger, split three ways by CP35 MULTIPLE A, fires all three 911s.

sounds.name: Distant Thunder Timpani
sounds.ref: In the style of Hector Berlioz — the four timpani of “Symphonie fantastique”, “Scène aux champs”, 1830
sounds.blurb: Soft, rumbling timpani rolls on F and C, like distant thunder, ending on single booming strokes.
sounds.how: A timpani head rings at its note with a partial a fifth above the octave, and it glides a touch flat as the head relaxes after the stroke. Here CM1A CV 1 plays a SINE and a TRIANGLE at 16’ and a quiet SINE at 8’ +7. The second 911, fired with every stroke from CM1A TRIG (lower), is split by CP35 MULTIPLE A: through an attenuator into the 921A’s second input, so each stroke starts sharp and settles, and into a second 902 that lets through a puff of low PINK NOISE, the felt mallet.

sounds.name: Syncopated Clock Woodblocks
sounds.ref: In the style of Leroy Anderson — “The Syncopated Clock”, 1945
sounds.blurb: A ticking, tocking pair of woodblocks with a skip in its step, and a little alarm bell at the end of every bar.
sounds.how: Row A plays the tick and the tock, an octave apart; row C, with 3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING on, halves the length of stages 5 and 6, so the clock hiccups. The woodblock’s envelope is fired from the 961’s left V-TRIG IN B, which holds the S-trigger for its SWITCH-ON TIME however long the clock’s pulse is: at its shortest, 40 ms, a crisp knock. Stage 8 OUT rings a bell on its own 911.

sounds.name: Lab Heartbeat
sounds.ref: In the style of Gil Mellé — the electronic score for “The Andromeda Strain”, 1971
sounds.blurb: A slow, deep heartbeat, lub-dub, lub-dub, over the faint, beating hum of laboratory machines.
sounds.how: The heart’s pacemaker is the 921 on SUB, a little over one beat a second. Its RECTANGULAR goes into the 961’s left V-TRIG IN B, which makes a 0.2 s S-trigger on every cycle, and CM1A TRIG resets the 921 so the first beat comes as the key goes down. The trigger is split by CP35 MULTIPLE A: the first 911 fires the lub at once, and the 911A passes it to the second 911 0.12 s later for the softer dub. Both open the same 902 on a deep sine.

steps.title: A pacemaker
steps.why:
The 921 on SUB, FREQUENCY −1.3, about 64 beats a minute; CM1A TRIG (upper) into its TRIG S. Its RECTANGULAR into the 961’s left V-TRIG IN B, SWITCH-ON TIME 3.5 (0.2 s); S-TRIG OUT through CP35 MULTIPLE A to the first 911.

- 961 SWITCH-ON TIME (left) 3.5 · 200 ms.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 5 · 140 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 5 · 140 ms.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (upper) to 921 TRIG S; 921 RECTANGULAR to 961 V-TRIG IN B (left) 1; 961 S-TRIG OUT (left) to CP35 MULTIPLE A (in); CP35 MULTIPLE A 1 to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN.

sounds.name: Dalek City Wind
sounds.ref: In the style of Tristram Cary — the electronic sound for “Doctor Who: The Daleks”, 1963
sounds.blurb: A desolate wind howling over a dead planet: gusts that rise and fall at no steady rate, whistling as they peak, with a thin draught keening through a crack.
sounds.how: Real wind never repeats, so no one LFO will do. Three slow oscillators at unrelated speeds, a 921B on LO, the 921 on SUB and another 921B on LO, go through three 995 attenuators into CP3A-O (1), which adds them: a wandering voltage that takes minutes to repeat. One of its outputs sweeps the 904A’s cutoff on PINK NOISE, with REGENERATION making it whistle; another opens and closes the 902, so the gusts swell and die. A third leads a thin, high draught through the 914.

steps.title: Pink noise that whistles
steps.why:
PINK NOISE through the 904A, REGENERATION 7, into the first 902, held half open by its FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE, to OUTPUT L. No envelope plays a part: the first 911’s knobs go back to their usual places.
- 904A: FREQUENCY RANGE 2, FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 1, REGENERATION 7.
- 902 (1) FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 3.
- 911 (1): T1 3 · 26 ms, T2 3 · 26 ms, E SUS 7 · 3.9 V, T3 3 · 26 ms.
- Cables: PINK NOISE 1 to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app).
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; CM1A TRIG (upper) from 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT from 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: a steady, hollow whistling roar.

- 921: COARSE RNG SUB, RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY −3.
- 921B (2): RANGE LO, FREQUENCY 5.

sounds.name: Slow Surf Swell
sounds.ref: In the style of Michel Redolfi — “Sonic Waters”, 1980s
sounds.blurb: Slow ocean waves: a roar building, breaking bright with a hiss of foam, and draining away into a quiet lull before the next one.
sounds.how: One very slow 921 sine, about one wave every eight seconds, is copied by CP35 MULTIPLE A three ways: through attenuators into the 904A, so each wave brightens as it breaks, into the first 902, so it swells, and into a second 902 for the foam. The 902’s gain stops at 0 V, so only the top half of the swell gets through the foam’s 902: a hiss that comes only at the crest. CM1A TRIG resets the 921 to a set point of its cycle, so the first wave starts building the moment the key goes down.

steps.title: The swell
steps.why:
The 921 on SUB, FREQUENCY −4.4, CLAMPING POINT 0.5; CM1A TRIG (upper) into its TRIG S. No envelope plays a part: the first 911’s knobs go back to their usual places. Its SINE into CP35 MULTIPLE A: one copy through 995 (1) attenuator 1 into the 904A’s CONTROL INPUT 1, one through attenuator 2 into the first 902’s CONTROL INPUT 1.
- 921: COARSE RNG SUB, RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY −4.4, CLAMPING POINT 0.5 · 14 %.
- 995 (1): ATTENUATOR 1 3, ATTENUATOR 2 6.
- 911 (1): T1 3 · 26 ms, T2 3 · 26 ms, E SUS 7 · 3.9 V, T3 3 · 26 ms.
- Cables: CM1A TRIG (upper) to 921 TRIG S; 921 SINE to CP35 MULTIPLE A (in); CP35 MULTIPLE A 1 to 995 (1) IN 1; 995 (1) OUT 1 to 904A CONTROL INPUT 1; CP35 MULTIPLE A 2 to 995 (1) IN 2; 995 (1) OUT 2 to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; CM1A TRIG (upper) from 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT from 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.

sounds.name: First Drops on a Roof
sounds.ref: In the style of Jack Foley — the studio sound effects of Hollywood, 1930s–50s
sounds.blurb: Heavy first raindrops of a storm plinking at no steady rate and each at its own pitch, over the hiss of rain on the street.
sounds.how: Three square LFOs at unrelated rates go into three of the 961’s left V-TRIG IN B jacks, which add together. The sum only rises past the trigger threshold when the second of the three goes high, which happens at no regular rate: each time, the 961 makes a 40 ms S-trigger and a drop falls. Each drop is a 921B sine whose pitch is pushed around by the 921 running a fast sawtooth into its AC MOD, so every drop lands on a different pitch, and the drop’s own 911 bends it down.

steps.title: A drop
steps.why:
The first 921B’s SINE at 2’ through the first 902 to OUTPUT L. Its 911 is split by CP3A-M (2) MULTIPLE A to the 902 and, through 995 (1) attenuator 1, to the 921B’s DC MOD.
- 921B (1): RANGE 2’, FREQUENCY 0.

sounds.name: Night Field Crickets
sounds.ref: In the style of Jana Winderen — insect and field recordings, “Energy Field”, 2010
sounds.blurb: Two crickets on a warm night, one high and fast, one lower and lazier, each chirping in bursts of rapid pulses.
sounds.how: A cricket’s chirp is a high tone chopped into pulses many times a second, and the pulses come in bursts. That is two amplitude modulations, so each cricket is two 902s in series: the first chopped by a RECTANGULAR at audio-ish speed (the 902’s gain stops at 0 V, so only the positive half opens it), the second by a slow RECTANGULAR on LO, cutting the trill into chirps. The first cricket’s song is the 921 at 1’; the second is a 921B at 2’.

- 921: COARSE RNG AUDIO, RANGE 1’, FREQUENCY 1.1.
- 921B (2): RANGE 32’, FREQUENCY −12.
- 911 (1): T1 3 · 26 ms, T2 3 · 26 ms, E SUS 7 · 3.9 V, T3 3 · 26 ms.

sounds.name: Hand-Cranked Siren

sounds.blurb: A hand-cranked siren winding up into a scream while the key is held, then sagging back down when it is let go, with the flutter of its rotor.
sounds.how: A hand siren speeds up while you crank and coasts down when you stop. The keyboard does not set the pitch here: CM1A TRIG (lower) fires the second 911 with a long attack and a long release, and that envelope, through an attenuator, is the first 921A’s pitch. So holding a key winds it up two octaves, and letting go lets it fall. The 921 at about 20 Hz, from its AUX OUT into the 902, is the rotor chopping the air.

sounds.name: Feedback Engine Revs

sounds.blurb: A rough, idling engine that roars up in revs while a key is held and drops back to a sputtering idle.

The 902 is held open by its FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE: the engine idles when nothing is played.

sounds.name: Pacific 231 Steam
sounds.ref: In the style of Arthur Honegger — “Pacific 231”, 1923
sounds.blurb: A steam locomotive pulling away: heavy chuffs that gather speed while the key is held, with a two-note whistle at the top of every cycle.
sounds.how: Each chuff is a burst of noise fired by the 960’s clock, with row A into the 904A making a heavy, light, medium, light pattern. The acceleration is a slow 911 into the 960’s CONTROL INPUT: one volt there doubles the clock, so as the envelope rises over three seconds the train goes from a crawl to four times as fast, and when the key lifts it coasts down. Stage 1 OUT blows the whistle, so it sounds more often as the train speeds up.

sounds.name: Thinking Machine Burble
sounds.ref: In the style of Tom Dissevelt and Kid Baltan — “Song of the Second Moon”, Philips, 1957
sounds.blurb: A 1950s electronic brain thinking aloud: a fast, stumbling burble of pitches with a metallic ring, speeding up and slowing down as you play.
sounds.how: The 960 on FREQUENCY RANGE 4 runs about 22 steps a second, too fast to hear as notes: a burble. Row A, on X2 so it covers four octaves, makes the pitches; row C, with 3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING on, gives every stage a different length, so the burble stumbles. The ring is a 902 used as a modulator: the burble into its SIG IN, a fixed 921B into its CONTROL INPUT, which multiplies one by the other. CM1A CV 2 goes into the 960’s CONTROL INPUT, so higher keys make it think faster.

steps.title: Twenty-two steps a second
steps.why:
Row A on X2 into the first 921A: a SINE at 4’ and a TRIANGLE a fifth up through CP3A-M (1) into the first 902. The clock runs on RANGE 4.
- 960: FREQUENCY RANGE 4, FREQUENCY VERNIER 2.8, ROW A RANGE X2.
- 960: ROW A STAGE 1 2, ROW A STAGE 2 7, ROW A STAGE 3 4, ROW A STAGE 4 9, ROW A STAGE 5 1, ROW A STAGE 6 6, ROW A STAGE 7 10, ROW A STAGE 8 3.
- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −1.
- 921B (1): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 0.
- 921B (2): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 7.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 5, GAIN 2 4, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: 960 ROW A OUTPUT 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) TRIANGLE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app).
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +; 911 (1) OUT from 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the 902 is shut.

steps.title: A 902 as a ring modulator
steps.why:
The fourth 921B on its own, SINE at 8’ +5, into the first 902’s CONTROL INPUT 1. CM1A TRIG (upper) fires the first 911 into CONTROL INPUT 2, so the key sets the depth.
- 921B (4): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 5.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 3 · 26 ms, E SUS 10 · 5.5 V, T3 4 · 60 ms.
- Cables: 921B (4) SINE to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1; CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 2.
- Listen for: a fast, metallic, ringing burble while the key is held.

steps.title: It stumbles, and you set its speed
steps.why:
3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING on, row C all over the place. CM1A CV 2 into the 960’s CONTROL INPUT.
- 960: 3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING On, ROW C RANGE X1.
- 960: ROW C STAGE 1 0, ROW C STAGE 2 6, ROW C STAGE 3 2, ROW C STAGE 4 9, ROW C STAGE 5 4, ROW C STAGE 6 1, ROW C STAGE 7 8, ROW C STAGE 8 3.

- Listen for: the burble stumbling, and running faster on the higher keys: a machine thinking.

sounds.name: Crystal Ray Gun
sounds.ref: In the style of Tim Blake — “Crystal Machine”, 1977
sounds.blurb: A space-rock ray gun: bursts of laser zaps diving down from a shriek, firing several times a second for as long as a key is held.
sounds.how: Each zap is one trigger: the first 911 opens the 902, the second sweeps the pitch down from three octaves above and drags the 904A down with it. The triggers come from the 921 on SUB at about eight a second, into the 961’s left V-TRIG IN B, so the gun keeps firing. The key does three things through CP35 MULTIPLE B: it sets the pitch, it resets the 921 so the first zap comes at once, and through the third 911 it opens a second 902, so the gun only fires while a key is down.

- 911 (2): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 4 · 60 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 4 · 60 ms.

sounds.name: Stack-to-Stack FM Bells
sounds.ref: In the style of Barry Truax — “Arras”, Vancouver, 1980
sounds.blurb: Glassy, clangorous FM tones that strike bright and inharmonic, then mellow into almost pure sines as they ring.
sounds.how: Frequency modulation at audio rate between the two oscillator stacks. The second stack, from CM1A CV 2, plays a SINE 5.8 semitones up, a ratio of about 1.4, which no harmonic series contains. It goes through the second 902, opened by its own fast 911, into the first stack’s AC MOD: the 902 sets the FM index. The index falls faster than the note, so each tone starts as a bright, clanging spectrum and melts into the carrier’s plain sine.

steps.title: The carrier
steps.why:
CM1A CV 1 to the first 921A: the first 921B’s SINE through the first 902 to OUTPUT L, struck by the first 911 and left to ring.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 7.5 · 1.2 s, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 7.5 · 1.2 s.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) SINE to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a pure, ringing sine.

steps.title: The modulator
steps.why:
CM1A CV 2 to the second 921A: the fourth 921B’s SINE, 5.8 semitones up, into the second 902, opened by the second 911 (fired by CM1A TRIG lower); its output through 995 (1) attenuator 1 into the first 921B’s AC MOD.
- 921B (4): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 5.8.
- 911 (2): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 6 · 330 ms.
- 995 (1) ATTENUATOR 1 3.
- Cables: CM1A CV 2 to 921A (2) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (2) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (4) LINK FREQ; 921B (4) SINE to 902 (2) SIG IN +; CM1A TRIG (lower) to 911 (2) S-TRIG IN; 911 (2) OUT to 902 (2) CONTROL INPUT 1; 902 (2) SIG OUT + to 995 (1) IN 1; 995 (1) OUT 1 to 921B (1) AC MOD.
- Listen for: a clanging, glassy strike that mellows into the sine.

sounds.name: Audio-Rate Sequencer Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Peter Zinovieff — EMS, “January Tensions”, London, 1968
sounds.blurb: A raw, buzzing bass with a hollow sub-octave under it, every waveform cycle built from the sequencer’s own steps.
sounds.how: Clocked at hundreds of hertz, the 960 is an oscillator. Four stages run (the rest on SKIP), and their stage OUTs into CP3A-M (1) at falling levels add up to a four-step staircase, one per four clock pulses: a crude sawtooth. CM1A CV 1 plus a fixed 2 V from CP3A-O (1) go into the 960’s CONTROL INPUT, so the keyboard plays it in tune. The 962, shifted by stage 4 OUT, flips between +6 V and −6 V once per cycle: a square an octave down.

steps.title: Four stages as a waveform
steps.why:
FREQUENCY RANGE 6, stages 5 to 8 on SKIP. Stages 1, 2 and 3 OUT into CP3A-M (1) at falling levels, then the 904A and the first 902 to OUTPUT L.
- 960: FREQUENCY RANGE 6, FREQUENCY VERNIER 7.3.
- 960: STAGE 5 MODE SKIP, STAGE 6 MODE SKIP, STAGE 7 MODE SKIP, STAGE 8 MODE SKIP.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 10, GAIN 2 6.6, GAIN 3 3.3, MASTER GAIN 6.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 1, REGENERATION 3.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 6 · 330 ms, E SUS 7 · 3.9 V, T3 4 · 60 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.
- Cables: 960 STAGE 1 OUT to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 960 STAGE 2 OUT to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; 960 STAGE 3 OUT to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 3; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); CM1A TRIG (upper) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.
- Unplug (Default patch): CM1A CV 1 from 921 FREQUENCY CONTROL INPUT 1; 921 SAWTOOTH from 902 (1) SIG IN +.
- Listen for: a buzzing, raw low C that ignores the keys for now.

steps.title: Play it in tune
