CM1A CV 1 into CP3A-O (1) CONTROL INPUT 1; CP35 +6 V 1 into its EXT INPUT, SWITCH 4 on, ATTENUATOR 3.3 (2 V). OUTPUT 1 into the 960’s CONTROL INPUT.

- Cables: CM1A CV 1 to CP3A-O (1) CONTROL INPUT 1; CP35 +6 V 1 to CP3A-O (1) EXT INPUT; CP3A-O (1) OUTPUT 1 to 960 CONTROL INPUT.

sounds.name: Three-Row Chance Melody
sounds.ref: In the style of Lejaren Hiller — the computer-chosen notes of the “Illiac Suite”, 1957
sounds.blurb: A plinking melody that seems to choose its notes by chance: it never quite repeats, wandering between three different scales.
sounds.how: Three rows of eight notes, but the melody never takes the same row for long: all three go into the 962, and the 962 is shifted not by the 960 but by the 921 on SUB, at a rate unrelated to the clock. So which row the pitch comes from changes at its own pace, now on one step, now in the middle of another, and the eight steps never line up with the switching the same way twice: a pattern hundreds of notes long from 24 knobs.

steps.why:

- 921A (1) FREQUENCY −1.
- 921B (2): RANGE 4’, FREQUENCY 0.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 6, GAIN 2 2, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 2, REGENERATION 2.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 5.5 · 220 ms, E SUS 0 · 0.0 V, T3 5 · 140 ms.
- Cables: 960 ROW A OUTPUT 1 to 921A (1) FREQUENCY IN 1; 921A (1) FREQUENCY TO 921B to 921B (1) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) LINK FREQ (to next) to 921B (2) LINK FREQ; 921B (1) TRIANGLE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 1; 921B (2) SINE to CP3A-M (1) INPUT 2; CP3A-M (1) OUTPUT + 1 to 904A SIG IN; 904A SIG OUT to 902 (1) SIG IN +; 902 (1) SIG OUT + to OUTPUT L (app); 960 OSCILLATOR OUTPUT to 961 V-TRIG IN A (left) 1; 961 S-TRIG OUT (left) to 911 (1) S-TRIG IN; 911 (1) OUT to 902 (1) CONTROL INPUT 1.

steps.title: The 962 chooses
steps.why:
Rows A, B and C into the 962’s SIG IN 1, 2 and 3; its OUTPUT 1 into the first 921A in place of row A. The 921 on SUB, a little under two cycles a second, its RECTANGULAR into the 962’s SHIFT.

sounds.name: Big-Band Stab and Fall
sounds.ref: In the style of Duke Ellington — the Ellington brass, “Cotton Tail”, 1940
sounds.blurb: A brassy six-note big-band chord punching out short stabs, and on the long notes the whole section falling off the end.
sounds.how: Six 921Bs voice a sixth-and-ninth chord on every key, the trumpets, trombones and saxes of a swing band. Its bite is a second 911 opening the 904A. The fall is arranged with the 911A: the key trigger reaches the third 911 only after half a second, so short stabs never get it. On a long note the third 911 rises, goes through CP3A-M (3), and its OUTPUT − sends it upside down into both 921As: the chord slides down.

sounds.name: Ballad Trumpet, Late Vibrato

Here the vibrato is the 921’s AUX OUT, already tiny, going through the third 902 before it reaches the first 921A. That 902 is opened by the third 911, and the third 911 is fired by the 911A a third of a second after the key: short notes stay straight, long notes bloom into vibrato.

sounds.name: Bebop Trombone Slides
sounds.ref: In the style of J. J. Johnson — “The Eminent Jay Jay Johnson”, 1953
sounds.blurb: A warm, buttery trombone playing a bebop line in F, every interval smeared by a quick slide.

CM1A CV 1 goes through its LOW PASS at the lowest setting, 10 Hz, before it reaches the 921A: every jump in pitch arrives as a smooth slide of about 50 ms, a trombone’s slide. The 904A, opened by a second 911 and following the keyboard, gives the brassy blat at the front of each note.

sounds.name: Tenor Sax Formants
sounds.ref: In the style of Dexter Gordon — “Go”, 1962
sounds.blurb: A big, breathy, slightly gritty tenor saxophone playing a lazy blues line in B flat.
sounds.how: A saxophone’s colour comes from fixed resonances of its body, its formants, which stay put whatever note is played. The 914 is fourteen fixed filters, so it can hold that shape: bands around 500 Hz and 1400 to 2000 Hz up, the very top and bottom down. The 914’s two INPUT jacks add, so breath noise from the 923 goes into the second one. A fast, very small wobble from the 921 into the pitch gives the tone its grit.

sounds.name: Syrinx Flute
sounds.ref: In the style of Jean-Pierre Rampal — Debussy’s “Syrinx” for solo flute, 1950s
sounds.blurb: A pure, sad solo flute drifting down through a chromatic phrase, with breath in the tone, a soft chiff on each note and a gentle vibrato.
sounds.how: A flute is nearly a sine, but what makes it a flute is the air: a steady breath around the tone and a puff of it at the start of each note, the chiff. The steady breath is PINK NOISE through both 923 filters in a row, a band, mixed in with the tone before the 902. The chiff is WHITE NOISE through its own 902 on a very short 911. A slow, small vibrato comes from the 921’s AUX OUT.

sounds.name: Rite Bassoon Solo
sounds.ref: In the style of Igor Stravinsky — the bassoon solo that opens “The Rite of Spring”, 1913
sounds.blurb: A strained, reedy bassoon singing high in its range: a long held C, a quick turn down and a sighing answer.
sounds.how: Stravinsky wrote his opening for the bassoon high above its comfortable range, where it sounds thin and strained. A bassoon’s formant sits around 500 Hz whatever it plays, so in the 914 the bands around 350 and 500 Hz are up and everything above 1400 Hz down: high notes lose their body exactly as they do on the instrument. A narrow RECTANGULAR gives the double reed’s nasal buzz.

sounds.name: Stranger Clarinet
sounds.ref: In the style of Acker Bilk — “Stranger on the Shore”, 1961
sounds.blurb: A warm, woody clarinet in its low register, crooning a slow, sentimental tune in F with a wide, lazy vibrato.
sounds.how: A clarinet’s bore gives it mostly odd harmonics, and a square wave is all odd harmonics. So the first 921B’s RECTANGULAR, with nothing at its LINK WIDTH, is a square, softened by a TRIANGLE. CM1A CV 2 into the 904A makes the cutoff follow the keyboard, so every note keeps the same warm colour instead of getting darker as it goes up. The 921’s AUX OUT gives Bilk’s wide, slow vibrato.

sounds.name: Uilleann Chanter and Drones
sounds.ref: In the style of Liam O’Flynn — uilleann pipes, “The Fox Chase”, 1970s
sounds.blurb: Irish uilleann pipes: a sweet, nasal chanter playing a slow air in D with quick grace notes, over the steady hum of three drones in octaves.
sounds.how: Pipes have no dynamics: the bag keeps the reed sounding at one level, so the chanter’s 911 is an organ’s on-off shape, and the ornaments are grace notes, not accents. The chanter is a narrow RECTANGULAR and a SAWTOOTH through the 914 with its upper-middle bands up, for the nasal sweetness. The drones are the second stack with nothing at its 921A: three 921Bs tuned to D in three octaves, through the 904A, held open by the second 902.

sounds.name: Cello Suite Prelude
sounds.ref: In the style of Yo-Yo Ma — Bach’s Cello Suite No. 1 in G, Prelude, 1983
sounds.blurb: A warm, singing solo cello flowing through the rocking arpeggios of Bach’s G major prelude, with a little bow noise and a gentle vibrato.
sounds.how: A cello’s warmth is its wooden body: fixed resonances that colour every note. The 914 plays the body here, with peaks around 250, 500 and 1000 Hz. Two SAWTOOTHs a few cents apart are the string, and PINK NOISE through the 923’s HIGH PASS is the rosin on the hair. The 904A follows the keyboard from CM1A CV 2, and the 921’s AUX OUT gives the vibrato. The quick attack lets the arpeggio speak but not snap.

sounds.name: Harpo Glissando
sounds.ref: In the style of Harpo Marx — his harp solos in the Marx Brothers films, 1930s
sounds.blurb: Shimmering harp glissandi sweeping up through each chord and ringing on the top note, the chord changing under your keys.
sounds.how: A glissando is too fast to play from a keyboard, but not from the 960. With 3RD ROW CONTROL OF TIMING on and ROW C RANGE X2, row C at 10 makes seven stages sixteen times faster than the clock, about twenty notes a second, and stage 8 at 0 holds at the clock’s own slow speed: a sweep up, then the top note left to ring. Row A arpeggiates a chord; CM1A CV 1 into the 921A’s second input moves it to whatever chord you hold.

sounds.name: Night Music Celesta
sounds.ref: In the style of Béla Bartók — “Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta”, 1936
sounds.blurb: A soft, glassy celesta playing a mysterious chromatic figure in octaves, each note a sweet chime with a bright glint that fades first.
sounds.how: A celesta is hammers striking steel bars over wooden resonators: almost pure sines with a bright, quickly fading glint. Bartók often doubled it in octaves, so here the first stack plays 8’ and 4’ sines together through one 902, ringing about a second. A third 921B, two octaves up and slightly sharp, the bar’s own glint, has its own 902 and a shorter 911, so it vanishes first.

sounds.name: Two-Part Harpsichord
sounds.ref: In the style of Wanda Landowska — Bach on the harpsichord, “Goldberg Variations”, 1933
sounds.blurb: A bright, jangling harpsichord playing two independent lines in G major at once, a running treble over a walking bass.
sounds.how: Counterpoint is two melodies at once, and the 960 has three rows. Row A plays the treble on the first stack, row B the bass on the second, both from the same clock and each with its own 911 and 902, so every step plucks two notes that make a consonance. A harpsichord’s registers are footages, like the 921Bs’ RANGE: the treble is an 8’ and a 4’ together, the bass 16’ and 8’. Narrow RECTANGULARs and SAWTOOTHs give the quill’s bright jangle.

sounds.name: Little Fugue Plenum
sounds.ref: In the style of E. Power Biggs — Bach’s “Little” Fugue in G minor on the organ, 1950s
sounds.blurb: A grand, bright pipe organ playing the subject of Bach’s “Little” Fugue, six ranks of pipes from 16’ to a high mixture, each note speaking with a little chiff.
sounds.how: A pipe organ’s stops are named by pipe length, 16’, 8’, 4’, and so are the 921Bs’ ranges. Six of them make a plenum: a 16’ bourdon, an 8’ principal, a 4’ octave, a 2⅔’ twelfth (4’ tuned up a fifth), a 2’ fifteenth and a 1⅓’ mixture rank (2’ up a fifth), each at its own level in the mixers. Real flue pipes speak with a puff of air, the chiff: WHITE NOISE through its own 902 on a very short 911.

sounds.name: Forward Roll Banjo
sounds.ref: In the style of Earl Scruggs — “Foggy Mountain Breakdown”, 1949
sounds.blurb: A bright, twangy five-string banjo picking a fast, rolling bluegrass pattern through G, C and D.
sounds.how: Three-finger banjo is a stream of eighth notes across the strings, the same roll in every chord: row A plays it, eight stages, root, third, fifth, the high drone and back. CM1A CV 1 into the 921A’s second input moves the whole roll to the chord you hold. The banjo’s twang is a thin pulse through the 904B, which takes out the body, and a 902 on EXP, which makes every note snap off.

sounds.name: Koto Oshide Bend
sounds.ref: In the style of Michio Miyagi — “Haru no Umi”, 1929
sounds.blurb: A delicate koto melody in a Japanese scale: bright plucks that ring and, on the held notes, bend up a whole tone as the player presses the string.
sounds.how: On the koto, the left hand presses the string behind the bridge to raise a note after it has been plucked: oshide. Here the 911A gives that delay. The key trigger is split by CP35 MULTIPLE A: one copy plucks the first 911 at once; the other only reaches the second 911 a third of a second later, and that 911, through an attenuator into the 921A’s second input, bends the pitch up by a whole tone. Quick notes are over before the press comes.

sounds.name: Jawari and Taraf Sitar
sounds.ref: In the style of Vilayat Khan — sitar, raga Yaman, 1960s
sounds.blurb: A buzzing, singing sitar climbing raga Yaman, each pluck zinging bright and settling, while the sympathetic strings shimmer awake behind it.
sounds.how: The sitar’s buzz, the jawari, is the string brushing a curved bridge, which piles the tone into a bright band that sweeps down as the note decays. Hard sync does the same: the second 921B is reset by the first one’s SAWTOOTH, and a fast 911 into its DC MOD sweeps it down from high above. The taraf, the sympathetic strings tuned to the raga, are the second stack on C, G and C. They are woken by the playing itself: the main voice goes into the 961’s AUDIO IN, which fires their 911 whenever the sitar sounds.

steps.title: The main string
steps.why:
CM1A CV 1 to the first 921A: the first 921B’s RECTANGULAR, and the second’s SAWTOOTH 7 semitones up, its SYNC on STRONG from the first one’s SAWTOOTH. Through CP3A-M (1), the 904A and the first 902 to OUTPUT L.
- 921B (2): RANGE 8’, FREQUENCY 7, SYNC STRONG.
- CP3A-M (1): GAIN 1 4, GAIN 2 6, MASTER GAIN 8.
- 904A: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE 2.5, REGENERATION 2.
- 911 (1): T1 0 · 2 ms, T2 7 · 780 ms, E SUS 2 · 1.1 V, T3 6.5 · 510 ms.
- 921 COARSE RNG SUB: the 921 plays no part in this sound, so it goes back to its LFO range.

sounds.name: Walking Bass in B Flat
sounds.ref: In the style of Paul Chambers — the bass on Miles Davis’s “Kind of Blue”, 1959
sounds.blurb: A round, woody upright bass walking quarter notes through two bars of a B flat blues, each note thumping and blooming.
sounds.how: A walking bass is one note a beat, chord tones and passing notes leading to the next chord: eight stages of row A are two bars. Row A goes into the first 921A, and the bass is a SINE and a TRIANGLE at 32’. An upright bass is plucked by a finger, a soft thump that blooms and fades, so a second 911 from the same clock pushes the 904A open briefly at the start of each note.
